From UNCTAD's perspective, we are ready to support member states through research, such as our upcoming creative economy outlook, technical assistance, including products such as the creative economy mapping that we recently did with Angola, and now being adapted to other countries, South-South cooperation together with our colleagues from UN Office for South-South Cooperation. We are happy to continue supporting particularly the champions of this process, of this agenda, like Indonesia, like Uzbekistan in the past, and of course, in this upcoming cycle committee season, as the substantive secretariat of the Creative Economy Resolution. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Juan Jose, for highlighting the new industries also, the focus on use, very important, especially for the countries of the South. but also some of those important aspects that we would need to take into account as we move forward with that. With the challenges of listening to our colleague from Namibia, the Deputy Permanent Representative of the mission would like to deliver the intervention and highlight the answers to those questions that we have raised. The floor is yours, Excellency, Mr. Nifiti Tikakau. Am I right?

Thank you so much. I appreciate it. Excellency Ambassador Hadi, Madame Bjork, Santhiay, good afternoon. And of course, our moderator, Madame Dima, director, excellencies here at the table, Ambassador of Mozambique, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. I have the honor to deliver the remarks that have been prepared by Director for Arts, Ms. Mkariko Amahulu. And just to go straight to the issue at hand is that from Namibia's perspective, the creative industries, of course, are particularly important because they give us an opportunity to build on something that we already have, indeed, with rich cultures, diverse heritage, talented people, powerful stories, and a young population that has enormous creative potential. The question for us is really, how do we turn those assets into meaningful and sustainable economic opportunities, particularly for our young people, women, local communities, and others who may not always have access to the mainstream economy. So this is something we're looking at quite deliberately. And in our sixth National Development Plan, which is called NDP6, this plan recognizes the importance of economic diversification and creating opportunities in new and emerging sectors. For us, the creative industries are part of that conversation. We see them not only as cultural sectors, cultural sector, but increasingly as a sector that can contribute to employment, entrepreneurship, and innovation in addition to inclusive economic growth. At the same time, we are implementing our Namibia Arts and Culture Heritage Policy and developing a creative and cultural industry strategy So this is something that we are busy with at the moment. And one of the important things for us is making sure that creative opportunities are not concentrated only in the capital city because of urbanization. Namibia is geographically a very large country, and many communities live far from major markets and economic centers. So access is a real issue. A talented young musician, filmmaker, designer, or craft producer in a rural community may have the talent, but not necessarily the connectivity, equipment, and the financing that was highlighted earlier by the distinguished ambassador, His Excellency, Ambassador of Mozambique, as well as training and market access that he also highlighted. So these are needed to ensure that the talent becomes a sustainable livelihood. So that is why we are looking at initiatives such as creative hubs and other infrastructure across the country, while also supporting local content development and strengthening opportunities across different creative sectors. I think we also have to be honest. Infrastructure alone is not enough. Many of our creators are producing incredible work, but the real challenge is often what happens after the work has been created, how do they reach markets, how do they protect their intellectual property, which is something that was also highlighted earlier by the distinguished Deputy Director or Director from Indonesia. How do they price their work, negotiate contracts, and ultimately earn sustainable income from their creativity? So for us, an important focus is building the entire value chain around creativity. We need to support creators, not only to create, but also to identify, protect, manage, commercialize, and monetize the intellectual and creative assets. And this becomes even more important in a digital environment. We are increasingly grappling with the issue of monetization in the online economy. Being online does not automatically mean earning an income. Creators can put their work online and reach audiences, but they still face challenges in converting views, streams, followers, and engagement into sustainable income. There are questions around payment systems, access to monetization, programs, platform requirements, and revenue sharing models. So the conversation cannot only be about getting our creators online. We also have to ask, once they're online, how do they actually generate and retain value from their work. This is particularly important because creative content can travel across borders very quickly, but the income generated from that content does not always return to the creator or the country where that content originated from. We therefore need to strengthen the capacity of our creators around digital business models, licensing, rights management, and online monetization, while also looking at how developing countries can have a stronger voice in shaping a more equitable global digital economy. At the same time, we should not assume that digitalization automatically means inclusion. Not everyone has reliable connectivity, access to devices, or the digital skills needed to participate fully in the online economy. So we need a balanced approach. We have to prepare our creators for the digital economy, But we also need to continue creating opportunities through physical spaces, community programs, local markets, and regional initiatives. We have to meet people where they are. And this brings me to the second question around South-South cooperation. I think it is important to recognize that South-South cooperation is broader than Africa-Asia cooperation. For Namibia, it means strengthening cooperation with our fellow African countries as well. There is already valuable experience within Africa in areas such as music, film, fashion, digital content, creative entrepreneurship, intellectual property, and creative hubs. We can learn from one another, both from what has worked and from what has not. There is a major opportunity to strengthen regional and continental markets. Our creative industries may be relatively small at national level, But when we connect our markets across Africa, the opportunities become much greater. Then, of course, there is the Asia-Africa dimension. Asian countries have developed interesting approaches to creative entrepreneurship, digital platforms, technology, intellectual property, and cultural exports, while Africa has enormous cultural assets, creative talent, and a young population. But I don't see this as simply Africa learning from Asia. It should be a two-way exchange. And I think we should extend that exchange to Latin America and the Caribbean. There is valuable experience there in music, film, cultural industries, creative entrepreneurship, cultural tourism, and the commercialization of cultural assets. Many across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean face similar challenges but have developed different approaches and solutions. That creates enormous opportunities for us to learn from one another. The key is that we need to move beyond conferences and declarations towards practical cooperation. That could mean partnerships beyond creative hubs and institutions, exchanges for creative entrepreneurs, joint training programs, technology transfer cooperation on intellectual property, new financing models, and importantly, better access to each other's markets. We should also cooperate on some of the challenges of the digital economy, particularly digital distribution, cross-border payments, intellectual property management, and the monetization of creative content. We need to ensure that our creators are not simply consumers or content providers on global platforms, but they are able to participate meaningfully and capture a fair share of the value they create. And I think this is where South-South cooperation can be practically or particularly powerful. We don't always have to start from scratch. There are countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and the Caribbean, and across the wider global South that are already developing solutions to challenges we are facing. The opportunities to learn from those experiences, adapt them to our own realities, and build practical partnerships. So for Namibia, the objective is to build creative ecosystems that are locally rooted, inclusive, and sustainable, but also globally connected. Ultimately, we do not lack creativity. The real challenge is creating the conditions that allow our people to turn that creativity into sustainable livelihoods. and ensuring that the value created by our cultures, knowledge, and our creative work is captured not only by platforms and intermediaries, but also by the creators and communities themselves. South-South cooperation can help us to do that faster by allowing us to learn from one another, share practical solutions, and build partnerships that are relevant to the realities of developing countries. And I thank you.

Thank you very much, Excellency. And thank you for underscoring the importance of the value chain, looking at it end to end, and of course, the many points that you raised, including on South-South cooperation. I think this is definitely also noted by us also on the flip side of of the equation and hopefully not only with the Global Alliance that we will launch, but I think we will also relay that message in terms of the need to have a strategic approach to South-South cooperation. And I think the UN entity on the ground can definitely help with that. Thank you very much. I know that we are a bit delayed, but that was due to the technical glitch. We do have WIPO, I think a lot of calls on intellectual property were raised by all the countries. So, Mr. Victor Vasquez Lopez, director of WIPO office here in New York, if you could shed the light on the role of WIPO that in terms of play or helping the countries to unlock the economic potential of the creative economy, including by enabling individual creators, creative MSMEs and local communities to protect, commercialize and derive greater value from their creative assets. and also to shed the light on the policy and institutional conditions that are needed to ensure that creators and the creative enterprises and local communities can effectively use the intellectual property system and benefit from it fully. The floor is yours.

Thank you. Thank you very much. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, it is an honor to be speaking on behalf of the World Intellectual Property Organization about the important topic of creative economy. Previous speakers have highlighted the impact of the creative economy in different areas, including Ambassador Hadi Mr. Bodillo Martinez, also the DPR just now from Namibia, on different areas. ASG Sankar referred to employment, to the impact on employment, and indeed the impact on employment of the creative economy is tremendous, 4% on global employment. with particularly a strong impact on young people and women. And this may seem paradoxical because we see creative activity as a very individual activity, a very solitary activity, a music composer, a writer works on her own. But then for that work to reach to the market, to the public, there has to be a publishing company, there has to be agents, bookshops, libraries. For music, there has to be bands, orchestras, instruments, radios, TV, concert halls, advertisements. So there is a rippling effect on employment, which is really tremendous. And intellectual property plays a vital role in the creative economy. It might be seen as the missing link between talent and development, because this intellectual property is what is going to facilitate that bridge towards market. If we look at copyright-based industries, we see that they account between 4% and 7% of GDP in countries like Mexico, Kenya, Philippines, Botswana, Indonesia, in 50 countries that we have surveyed. So what is the role of WIPO to address the creative economy? To support the creative economy, we take an integrated ecosystem approach, combining technical assistance, policy dialogue, community engagement, institutional partnerships, and cross-regional cooperation. First, we help creators understand and use IP through projects on the ground, capacity building, and learning platforms. CLIP, Creators Lane Intellectual Property is an example of this, a free to use online learning platform where experienced musicians and mentors help creators make better business choices. This peer network approach is also used by the WIPO Fantastic Agents of the Creative Economy, known as WIPO FACE, a global community connecting creators, artists, entrepreneurs, experts, and partners. It supports networking, peer learning, mentorship, and policy advocacy, helping creators and micro, small, and medium enterprises understand and use IP in their communities. Indonesia offers a good example of this. ecosystem integrated approach, as illustrated by initiatives developed in the country, such as Animate and Innovate with IP, a WIPO-supported project designed to strengthen the ability of the next generation of Indonesian creators to develop, protect, commercialize, and license IP assets. Second, WIPO fosters knowledge sharing. IP lies at the core of the creative economy, and knowledge sharing is crucial to ensuring that creators can fully benefit from it. Through one-day IP workshops and other programmes, WIPO equips creators, start-ups and MSMEs to manage IP as a strategic business asset and learn from one another's experience. Just last week, we held a workshop supporting innovators selected through the 2026 UN Call for Innovations for the SDGs Challenge, co-convened by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs. But capacity building alone is not enough. Creators need also accessible IP services, coherent policies, capable institutions, finance, and pathways to markets. WIPO's creative ecosystem diagnostic model helps countries build a shared evidence-based understanding of their creative economies by examining the institutional environment, resources for creative production and outputs demonstrating economic impact. The model is used in more than 50 countries and with regional partners and it identifies the strengths, gaps, and opportunities so that governments can design more targeted policies, institutions, and IP frameworks for their creative economy. This also creates a practical basis for South-South and triangular cooperation. Countries can compare evidence, which is a standardized exchange experience, adapt successful models, and build cross-regional partnerships. This cross-regional approach can strengthen IP management, valuation and commercialization, improve access to markets and finance, and help transform creative assets into viable and investable opportunities. The World Conference on Creative Economy, initiated and hosted by Indonesia, demonstrates this spirit of cooperation. WIPO has partnered in this effort since the third conference in Bali in 2018, The fifth edition of the conference to be held in Jakarta in October 2026 will provide another opportunity to advance global and South-South dialogue on creativity, innovation and IP. During the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, WIPO will also highlight two initiatives that demonstrate how IP can support both the creative economy and the broader innovation ecosystem. And we are cordially invited to both of them. The first event on 18 September will highlight the WIPO Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure Interchange Initiative, known as AIII, a multi-stakeholder dialogue which seeks to ensure that creators can identify, credit and support their content as AI evolves, strengthening the infrastructure that underpins a sustainable and thriving creative economy. The second event on September 21st will highlight the WIPO Green Initiative, which connects innovators, entrepreneurs, researchers and businesses to help commercialize and scale green technologies, transforming ideas and IP into sustainable economic and social value. In closing, I would like to highlight that intellectual property is fundamental to the creative economy and South-South cooperation, as was recognized by many of the speakers previously. It turns creativity into jobs, exports, and finance. These contributions support the UN General Assembly Resolution 7833 on promoting the creative economy for sustainable development and advance the 2030 agenda. WIPO extends, stands ready to partner with member states, creators and local communities through practical country led tools tailored to different contexts. Together, we can ensure that the creative economy becomes a more inclusive, sustainable and impactful pillar of development. I thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Lopez. for sharing WIPO's approaches, including this integrated system approach, and for inviting everybody for the two upcoming events. I think it will be very informative. With this, we come to a conclusive end to this very interesting discussion. And I think there is a lot of key messages that came out of this discussion today. First, we all agree and with all the interventions that the creative economy is part of the economic diversification, the enterprise development, digital transformation, employment and social inclusion. It is therefore needs to be reflected and mainstream development, trade, investment, education, technology and local development policies. Second, we need to connect creativity with value. Protecting intellectual property is essential, but protection alone is not enough. Developing countries also need capacity for valuation, financing, commercialization, fair remuneration, data, and access to markets. And third, South-South cooperation can help countries move faster by sharing institution and policy approaches, skills, technologies, and market connections that have already been tested in comparable context. The objective is not to reproduce a model, but to adapt experiences with country ownership and cultural context at the center. And fourth, inclusion must be designed into the ecosystem. Women, young people, local communities, individual creators, and micro and small enterprises should not remain at the margin of digital platforms, finance, or global value chains. So the next milestone is actually Jakarta. The fifth World Conference on Creative Economy provides an opportunity to move from recognition to implementation. And I hope that the Jakarta vision will capture the priorities voiced today and translate them into concrete partnerships, peer learning arrangements and pathways for investments and market access. And here also encouraging each institutions represented here today to carry forward one recommendations and one partnership proposal from this room to Jakarta, subject to the necessary consultations. We also stand ready to help and put our platforms at the service of all the member states. Thank you very much, Excellencies. And with this, we conclude this discussion. Thank you.
